title: The parable of the vine-growers
english: On the parable of the vine-growers. When the wise men of the people saw the Son, they were not entirely without perception of their own superiority, and they supposed him to be the heir. They even dare to kill him, so that they themselves might become masters of the vineyard. They cast him out and killed him; and immediately the Lord of the vineyard arrives, having risen from the dead, and destroys the evil vine-growers utterly, and hands the vineyard over to other vine-growers, the apostles. Then he answers from the prophecy that he was rejected by those men, but with God he is honored and the head of the corner: "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits" (Matthew 21:43).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B.
Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Origen is commenting on the parable of the vineyard in Matthew 21, where the wise men of the people see the Son and plot to kill him so they can keep the vineyard.

title: Comparison of parables where God is called a man
english: A comparison of the parables in which God is called a man. In the parable of the workers, a father who is a householder goes out to hire. In the parable of the dinner and the weddings of the son, he has been named a king—for he is greater than a father who is a householder, as one sending an army. In Luke, "a man planted a vineyard" (Luke 20:9); and in Mark likewise. In many ways in the Scriptures God is taken as a man; it makes a great difference whether he is named simply a man, or a householder, or a king. Glory to Christ. Amen.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B.
Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Origen is closing his treatment of the parable of the vineyard by comparing how God is depicted as a human figure in different Gospel parables.
